Yeah, I used ServiceNow at my previous stop, Thermo Fisher. It was a very large implementation—about a $40B company with roughly 2,000 sites. We handled around 2M tickets annually. The modules we used included Incident, Request, Problem, Change, and Knowledge. We had a full Configuration Management Database (CMDB), Asset Management, and Major Incident Management. We also used HR—many HR service requests ran through ServiceNow. And we started implementing GRC as another module.

The key drivers were faster resolution of IT tickets and reducing MTTR. We were on, I believe, Zendesk at the time, and needed better, faster performance and improved routing. We also needed centralized management of all IT assets. So, multiple drivers, but really it was about improving service levels (SLAs), MTTR, and the user experience from an IT perspective.

Yes, it was about consolidating a lot of the IT tools—some of it was even paper-based. We wanted to improve service levels and MTTR and also be able to track our assets. In addition, we wanted better compliance—we’re subject to heavy regulations such as SOC, ISO, GxP, and SOC 2. ServiceNow can help with controls around our IT assets and equipment, so that was another driver.

The module was GRC—Governance, Risk, and Compliance. Basically, you can load all of your risks. For example, if you haven’t done a pen test on a server in a while, that’s a risk because the system hasn’t been stress-tested for security. That would be logged in the GRC module as a risk, then categorized and prioritized. And could you repeat the other part of your question?

For asset management, we needed better inventory of our assets to support lifecycle management. For HR, they were handling a lot of tickets via phone, paper, and email, so we needed a consolidated system to improve service delivery and tracking from an HR perspective. Those were two big drivers.

The pain points really started at the site and division levels, and then it became a strategic digital transformation initiative. There were a lot of complaints about slowness—in both the process and service levels—which weren’t great. This was observed at the lower levels, typically at the site level, the manufacturing plants. They have a site lead and an IT partner. From there, you go up to the divisions, where you have a division lead. Once we started seeing commonality across sites and divisions, it moved up to a strategic initiative from an IT global perspective. So, it started at the site level, grew into a strategic IT initiative, and then was implemented globally.

Great question. I’ve been with Abzena for about 6 months, and that decision was made by my predecessor. We actually had ServiceNow at one point, but they felt that for the size of the company it was too complicated for end users. They also wanted to take advantage of AI, so this custom solution integrates with Microsoft Teams—you can talk to it, and it can create a ticket. It has AI capabilities to recognize an IT issue, try some troubleshooting, and if it can’t resolve it, it creates a ticket. At that time, ServiceNow’s agents weren’t as advanced, and this was more simplified. The backend is also easier to manage. Personally, I’m not sure why they made the move—I think it was poorly implemented and then they decided to switch. Not my decision; it predated me and we have to live with it. One repercussion is we don’t really have asset management for all our IT assets, which is a big pain point for me right now. We’re now looking at possibly implementing just the ServiceNow asset management piece to categorize all our GMP equipment and IT assets. I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.

Yes. Number one, the system was validated. For example, when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have. It provided more robust functionality for a typical GxP-related change. Typically, you have an IT change that then goes to Quality; Quality opens a change, it gets approved and reviewed, you might have to do testing, etc. ServiceNow offered more customization and out-of-the-box functionality than Zendesk, including advanced routing and workflows to accommodate GxP processes.

Sure. We're on BMC Helix ITSM, cloud-hosted, and we use Incident, Problem, Change, Service Request Management, Knowledge, and the CMDB. We also use Helix Digital Workplace as the front end for employees. We don't have the full AIOps suite turned on yet - that's something we're evaluating. We handle somewhere around 60,000 tickets a year across roughly 2,200 employees and about a dozen manufacturing and lab sites.

A few things. The legacy tool - an old ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus instance - just wasn't scaling. It was slow, the reporting was weak, and it didn't have a real CMDB, so we had no reliable asset inventory for our lab equipment or IT hardware. We were also getting pressure from Quality and Regulatory to have better audit trails on changes, since a lot of our systems touch GxP-relevant processes. So it was really scalability, asset visibility, and compliance-grade change control.

It started as an IT-driven project, honestly. I inherited the legacy tool and it was falling apart - outages, tickets getting lost. Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated, and our VP of IT and our Head of Quality co-sponsored it. So it became bigger than just an IT refresh, but it wasn't part of some grand ERP-style transformation program.

The big one is the change approval workflow tied to GxP flags. When someone opens a change, they tag whether it's GxP-impacting, and that routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation. We also get a full audit trail - who approved what, when, what the change actually was - which is exactly what our auditors want to see. The old tool had none of that; changes were tracked in email half the time.

We use Incident, Service Request, Change, Problem, Asset Management, and we recently turned on the Project module for some larger infrastructure rollouts. We're fully cloud, obviously - Freshservice doesn't really do on-prem. We handle somewhere around 18,000 tickets a year across about 450 employees, plus a rotating pool of field contractors who submit requests through email-to-ticket.

Honestly, it was chaos. Nothing was tracked, nothing had an SLA, and when we started scaling up project development, leadership wanted actual metrics - how fast we're resolving things, how many devices we have deployed in the field, that kind of thing. We also started doing SOC 2 work for some of our financing partners, and having zero audit trail on IT changes was a real gap.

Mostly IT and security-driven at first. It became more strategic once the SOC 2 requirement came from our CFO's office - that got leadership attention pretty fast.

We looked at competitors like Jira. We also considered that Workday had some ticket management capabilities. We looked at Zendesk again. We actually looked at quite a few different systems. The biggest ones were Jira, BMC’s tool, and a few others I’m blanking on.

The first thing is functionality.

Functionality. Next was user experience. Then how the system scales—can it support growth within 3-5 years? We also looked at integration—can it integrate with our identity and access management (IAM), with Workday (our HR/HCM system)? We also considered automation—what can it do in terms of automatic routing, etc. There was reporting and analytics, total cost of ownership, and some softer considerations like vendor reputation.

I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership. Fourth, the user experience. And fifth, customization.

First, we’d want a live demo of the capabilities. From there, we might ask for customer references, but we’d start with a product demonstration to show they truly have the capabilities. Next, a short POC to prove it. For example, on integration, we’d ask, can you integrate with Workday? If they said yes in the demo, we’d say, show us. In their environment, they’d run a small POC: here’s ServiceNow integrated with Workday—when a new employee is onboarded, it flows right into the ServiceNow process.

They had strong integration and strong scalability. They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.

Go ahead.

I’d say scalability. We were at a point where the volume of data and manual workflows in our previous system wasn’t scalable. When we left it, we were at around 2M tickets per year, and trying to do that on the previous system would just break it. So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.

At the time, Jira wasn’t scalable enough and lacked modules we needed. We were concerned that at 1-2M tickets we’d hit performance issues. Jira is great for agile software project management, but we worried about handling infrastructure issues, major incident management, and change management. Zendesk is very intuitive for customer service and fits small to mid-market needs, but it lacks advanced workflow automation and customization. We were already seeing performance issues as our data volume grew.

If we set ServiceNow at about $100 per user/month as a baseline, I’d put Zendesk at roughly $50-55. Jira was very inexpensive but lacked capabilities—around $20-21. So compared to Zendesk, ServiceNow was almost double.

The business case focused on scalability. We were growing—from roughly a $20B company to about $30B—and adding around 10-50K users. We were already seeing performance issues, and ticket management wasn’t meeting GMP/GxP requirements. That case was presented to finance mainly to confirm budget alignment, but the real decision-makers were senior IT leadership. Directors and senior directors typically drive the business case; a global IT senior director/director helps assemble it. Approval then goes to the VP level. Depending on the spend, the CIO may also sign off, but that’s primarily to confirm budget and due diligence. Most of the influence and decision-making happens at the director, senior director, and VP levels.

For integration, I’d rate ServiceNow 9/10. Zendesk 6/10. Jira 7/10. BMC 7/10.

Total cost of ownership would come down to this: ServiceNow is very expensive—I'd put it at a 6. Jira is very economical—I'd give it a 9. Zendesk is probably a 7. And BMC is also very expensive—maybe a 7.

Yeah, good question. For user experience, I would say Jira has a really strong user experience; I'd give it an 8 out of 10. Zendesk is very simple—it's a pretty simplified and easy-to-use experience, and so is the backend—so I'd give it an 8. ServiceNow can have its complexity depending on how you configure it, so I'd give it a 7. And then BMC is probably a little bit easier to use; I'd give it an 8.

Yeah, good question. ServiceNow: a 9—you can customize pretty much everything with ServiceNow. Jira has some customization; I'd probably put it at a 6. Zendesk: a 6 as well. BMC offers more customization—maybe an 8.

We looked at ServiceNow, Ivanti Neurons for ITSM, and Freshservice. We also briefly looked at Jira Service Management but ruled it out pretty early - it just didn't have the depth we needed for CMDB and compliance workflows.

Cost was definitely near the top, just given our size - we're not a $40 billion company, we're a few hundred million in revenue. Beyond cost, it was implementation speed, how well it could support GxP-style approval workflows out of the box, integration with our existing systems like SAP and Workday, and honestly, how painful the admin experience would be for a small team, since I only have three people supporting the platform.

Let me think. First would be total cost of ownership. Second, out-of-the-box support for compliance workflows. Third, implementation speed. Fourth, integration capability. And fifth, ease of administration for a small team.

We asked all four vendors for detailed multi-year quotes, not just year-one pricing, because we'd heard stories about year-two and year-three increases. ServiceNow's rep was actually pretty transparent about the escalation, Ivanti gave us a three-year lock, and BMC gave us a similar multi-year commitment. Freshservice was cheapest but their compliance workflow story was thinner, so it dropped down our list fast.

Honestly, it came down to price relative to capability. ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally. Ivanti was close in price to BMC, but their compliance and change-approval workflows needed more custom configuration to meet our GxP requirements. BMC had more of that baked in already from working with other pharma and med device customers. So BMC gave us the best balance of cost and compliance readiness.

We looked at ServiceNow, Ivanti since I had experience with it, Zendesk, and Freshservice. We ruled out ServiceNow pretty quickly on cost; it felt like way more platform than we needed at our size.

Cost was number one, no question, given our size. After that, speed of implementation, ease of use for a non-technical field workforce, asset management capability since we track a lot of hardware across remote sites, and integration with our existing tools, mainly Azure AD and Intune.

First, cost. Second, ease of use. Third, implementation speed. Fourth, asset management depth. Fifth, integration with Azure AD and Intune.

Zendesk felt built more for customer support than internal IT - the asset management piece was weak. Ivanti I already knew from my last job, and honestly it wasn't a great memory - clunky admin, slow to configure. Freshservice hit the sweet spot: modern interface, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a price point that made sense for us.

Probably BMC comes closest.

Customization, scalability, and integration.

Yes, agreed.

I'm very impressed with their CEO. He's significantly grown the company's market cap [AUDIO UNKNOWN] and has a strong vision. They had some poor leadership in the past, and he's really turned the company around. I admire that they're leaning headfirst into AI—now they have agents, and with the Moveworks acquisition as well. They're driving a major digital transformation from what was just an ITIL system into HR and broader service management, and now they want to get into the CRM space. I think they're well-positioned to compete against Salesforce. Overall, the functionality and scalability are very strong.

We have dedicated admins who maintain it, customize it, and create new flows, so there is ongoing work. You can also engage partners to help. There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system. You need dedicated admins, and partners for more advanced configurations and integrations.

It's a good question. I'd point to BMC as one example. Obviously, cost is number one—many competitors are lower cost. But they typically don't have as much capability and flexibility as ServiceNow. Jira is making a run at AI, which makes it quite competitive. And Zendesk is simple—they keep the user experience simple, which makes it easier for users and simpler to maintain with straightforward workflows. That's an advantage.

Yeah, well said.

At the time, they weren’t leaning into it as heavily; the vendor we chose was taking an AI-first approach. That was the major difference. Since then, I think they’ve grown in their AI capabilities. Cost was also a factor—we saw lower licensing costs.

It was about 3-5 employees, each allocated around 30-40% of their time to maintain the system. For more complex needs—major upgrades or complex flows—we engaged partners. Did that impact ROI? Slightly, but we were able to scale to the point where it still made sense.

Integration - I'd give ServiceNow a 9, BMC an 8, Ivanti a 7, and Freshservice a 6. ServiceNow's ecosystem of connectors is just bigger.

TCO - flip it around. Freshservice would be a 9, BMC an 8, Ivanti a 7, and ServiceNow a 5, just given how expensive it gets at scale.

Freshservice is probably the easiest, I'd say 9. BMC I'd give a 7 - it's manageable for my small team but there's a learning curve. Ivanti is similar, maybe a 7. ServiceNow is powerful but complex, I'd put it at a 6 for a team our size.

BMC I'd rate an 8 for us specifically, because of the pharma-specific templates they had available. ServiceNow is probably a 9 in raw capability, but you have to build a lot of it yourself. Ivanti is a 6 - doable, but more custom work. Freshservice is weaker here, maybe a 4; it's really built more for lighter-weight IT support use cases.

Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality. Where BMC pulled ahead was specifically in how much pre-built compliance content they had for regulated industries.

Yes, that's fair. When we needed a specialized integration, our BMC partner pool was smaller, and it sometimes took longer to find someone who'd done exactly what we needed. With ServiceNow, there's just a much bigger community and more integrators to choose from.

For us specifically, the out-of-the-box compliance templates and the fact that BMC's account team had deep pharma and med device experience. They understood our GxP language without us having to explain it from scratch, which sped up implementation.

Freshservice, I'd give a 9. Zendesk's also strong there, an 8. ServiceNow I'd put at a 6 - powerful but a lot to configure. Ivanti, from my prior experience, maybe a 5.

Freshservice a 9, Zendesk an 8, Ivanti a 7, ServiceNow a 4 for a company our size.

ServiceNow's probably the strongest on paper, I'd give it a 9, but it's overkill for us. Freshservice I'd say a 7 - solid discovery agent, good enough for our needs. Ivanti's asset piece was actually decent, maybe a 7 as well. Zendesk is weak here, a 3.

Freshservice, an 8 - the Azure AD sync was pretty painless. ServiceNow's probably a 9 in raw capability. Ivanti was a 6 in my experience, lots of manual config. Zendesk, maybe a 5.

Zendesk, probably, on ease of use and general user experience. Where Freshservice pulls ahead is asset management and the IT-specific workflows - ITIL processes that Zendesk just isn't built around.

Yeah, that's fair. We're starting to feel some of that as we've added more complex approval chains for the Project module. It's not a hard wall, but you notice the automation builder gets clunky once you're chaining a lot of conditional logic.

Cost, hands down, and time to value. We were live in about ten weeks. I don't think we'd have been live on ServiceNow in under six months, and it would've cost multiples of what we paid.

Great question. The implementation was quite complex and took roughly 9-12 months to fully complete. The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required. User testing wasn’t clearly defined, so we had to pull in resources who weren’t expecting it, and it was hard to secure their time.

It integrated well, but it took time to build. We set up single sign-on with Active Directory and integrated Workday. It wasn’t plug-and-play; our engineers and identity access management team had to do quite a bit of work. There was a lot of back-and-forth on APIs, customization, changes on both sides, and permissions.

No—at the time that wasn’t available, so it was mostly custom work using direct APIs.

They had some out-of-the-box APIs, but we had legacy systems and tools that those APIs wouldn’t connect to, so we built a middle layer to make them talk. For example, we wanted to bring in Databricks data related to certain service tickets. There was a Databricks connector, but a lot of our legacy ERP data was feeding Databricks and the connector didn’t have access to it, so we wrote a custom API to integrate the two.

Great question. I think it was a combination of both—working with ServiceNow and an integrator. There should be some commonality between ServiceNow’s preferred playbook and what partners are doing. Somewhere between how ServiceNow used to run implementations and how partners operate today, there are gaps. I think there’s misalignment between ServiceNow and the partner ecosystem on how long things really take. Partners need to be clearer about the level of effort required and what the implementation plan looks like. For a concrete example, we expected a 6-7 month implementation, and it ended up taking 9-12 months—roughly another quarter we had to absorb.

It took about seven months from kickoff to go-live, which was faster than I expected going in. The biggest challenge was data migration - pulling asset and ticket history out of the legacy ManageEngine tool. The export tools weren't great, so we ended up doing a lot of manual cleanup and mapping before we could load it into the new CMDB. The second challenge was change management with end users - a lot of site-level staff had used the old portal for years and were resistant to a new interface.

Workday integration was fairly smooth - BMC had a solid connector for HR data sync, onboarding and offboarding trigger workflows. SAP was harder. We use SAP for some inventory and equipment data that we wanted reflected in the CMDB, and there wasn't an out-of-the-box connector that fit our SAP configuration, so our internal team built a custom API integration. That took an extra six or seven weeks we hadn't originally budgeted.

A mix. For Workday it was mostly BMC's native connector. For SAP it was custom REST API work built by our integration engineer, because our SAP instance is fairly customized on the inventory side.

Mostly complaints about the portal looking different and people not knowing where to submit certain request types. We ran a series of lunch-and-learns at each site and recorded short walkthrough videos. It took about two months post-go-live before ticket volume through the correct channels stabilized.

Like I said, about ten weeks from contract to go-live. The biggest challenge honestly wasn't the platform - it was getting field staff to actually use tickets instead of texting or calling me directly. We had to do a real change management push, incentivize adoption, that kind of thing.

Azure AD sync for user provisioning was straightforward, native integration, took maybe a day to configure. Intune was a bit more work - we wanted device data flowing into the asset CMDB, and we ended up using a combination of the native integration plus some manual scripting to get certain custom fields to map correctly.

Mostly the marketplace apps for the core stuff - Azure AD, Slack for notifications, a couple of monitoring tool integrations. The custom scripting was really just for those extra Intune fields I mentioned.

Can you repeat the question?

As I mentioned before, ServiceNow’s implementation total cost of ownership was roughly double compared to its competitors.

In terms of expectations, the biggest miss was the internal level of effort and commitment—pulling additional resources for testing and validation. I’d say that added another 20-30% in cost. It’s soft cost, but we had to pull those resources away from other tasks.

A bit of both - Freshservice's native reporting is decent for standard use cases, but for a very specific custom compliance format, it just doesn't flex enough without going into their analytics add-on, which we haven't purchased.
Yeah, I agree. I think that's really well put. That aligns well with my experience.
Yes. Yes, we're struggling now. We got rid of ServiceNow, and that left a gap in terms of asset management.

That's a good point—that once you're implementing something as big as this, it's very difficult to switch. However, I do like where the company is going, and I think ServiceNow met the scalability challenges we were facing. We got the integrations we needed, as well as the automated workflows. Overall, once we got it implemented, it worked well.

I would push back and question why that's the case. Cost might be one reason, but I would look at scalability, integration, and especially compliance from a regulatory perspective. We would look at things quite differently.

Yes, it would. Switching would be very difficult. On a scale of 1 to 10, it's not as difficult as an ERP system—I'd put ERP at 10, a multi-million-dollar project that takes 2-3 years to switch. This would be around 7-8. You'd still make a significant investment, around $1M-$1.5M, and invest a lot of time—at least a year for implementation.

On a 1 to 10 scale, I'd put it around a 6. It's not as entrenched as something like an ERP, but we've built a fair amount of custom CMDB structure and compliance workflow logic that would need to be rebuilt or migrated.

Definitely cost—lower implementation cost and leaning into AI. And if they could port the data from ServiceNow to one of those systems and reduce implementation time, that would be significant.
Yes.

Probably ServiceNow at this point, just because if we're going to absorb switching costs anyway, I'd want the platform with the broadest long-term ecosystem and AI roadmap, assuming budget allowed it.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three run cloud ITSM suites on the same core modules but at radically different scales — ~2M tickets a year at a $40B pharma manufacturer versus 60,000 and 18,000. All three replaced a failing or absent legacy system for the same three reasons: scalability, asset visibility, and audit-grade compliance. Each tells the same origin story: an IT-level fix that turned strategic only once compliance risk was named.

canonical_quote.quote: So it was really scalability, asset visibility, and compliance-grade change control.

agreements.statement: The purchase was driven by a legacy tool that could not scale, combined with the absence of a reliable asset inventory and no audit trail on IT changes.

positions.gist: Zendesk was too slow with weak routing and no centralized asset management; compliance regimes (SOC, ISO, GxP) added pressure.

citation.quote: We also needed centralized management of all IT assets.

positions.gist: ManageEngine wasn't scaling, had no real CMDB, and Quality/Regulatory wanted better change audit trails.

citation.quote: It was slow, the reporting was weak, and it didn't have a real CMDB, so we had no reliable asset inventory for our lab equipment or IT hardware.

positions.gist: Nothing was tracked at all, no SLAs, and SOC 2 work exposed the absence of change audit trails.

citation.quote: Nothing was tracked, nothing had an SLA, and when we started scaling up project development, leadership wanted actual metrics

agreements.statement: The initiative began inside IT and was only elevated to a strategic/leadership priority once it was reframed around regulatory or audit risk.

positions.gist: Started as site-level complaints about slowness, rolled up through divisions, then became a global strategic IT initiative.

citation.quote: So, it started at the site level, grew into a strategic IT initiative, and then was implemented globally.

positions.gist: IT-driven until a compliance-risk business case won co-sponsorship from the VP of IT and Head of Quality.

citation.quote: Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated, and our VP of IT and our Head of Quality co-sponsored it.

positions.gist: IT and security-driven until the CFO's office imposed SOC 2, which drew leadership attention quickly.

citation.quote: It became more strategic once the SOC 2 requirement came from our CFO's office - that got leadership attention pretty fast.

agreements.statement: A GxP flag on the change record that routes to Quality for review/approval is described as the single most valuable regulated-industry capability, and both note the prior tool tracked changes in email or not at all.

positions.gist: A GxP checkbox on a change triggers specific routing and workflow into Quality that Zendesk could not do; the system was validated.

citation.quote: when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have.

positions.gist: GxP tagging routes changes to Quality for electronic signature before implementation, with a full audit trail for auditors.

citation.quote: The old tool had none of that; changes were tracked in email half the time.

conflicts.statement: Whether a heavyweight platform like ServiceNow is appropriate below enterprise scale: expert-1's current small employer removed ServiceNow as too complicated for end users and now regrets losing asset management, while expert-2 built a comparable compliance capability at similar size on another platform.

positions.gist: Calls the predecessor's move off ServiceNow poorly thought through and non-scalable, and is now looking to buy back just the asset module.

citation.quote: I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.

positions.gist: Chose BMC Helix at ~2,200 employees and is satisfied with the compliance-grade change control it delivers.

citation.quote: We're on BMC Helix ITSM, cloud-hosted, and we use Incident, Problem, Change, Service Request Management, Knowledge, and the CMDB.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-1 is comparing against a 2,000-site $40B implementation and inherited a decision he did not make; expert-2 designed for a few-hundred-million-dollar company from the start.

outliers.gist: Only interviewee speaking from two vantage points — a 2M-ticket, 2,000-site ServiceNow estate at Thermo Fisher plus a small custom AI/Teams tool at Abzena he inherited and dislikes.

citation.quote: We actually had ServiceNow at one point, but they felt that for the size of the company it was too complicated for end users.

outliers.gist: Only non-pharma driver set: SOC 2 for financing partners rather than GxP, and a field/contractor workforce submitting via email-to-ticket.

citation.quote: plus a rotating pool of field contractors who submit requests through email-to-ticket

notable: Ticket-to-employee ratios differ sharply: expert-2 reports ~60,000 tickets across ~2,200 employees versus expert-3's ~18,000 across ~450 — useful context when reading their scale complaints.
Only expert-1 reports modules beyond core ITSM: HR service delivery and a GRC rollout for logging and prioritizing risks such as overdue pen tests.

expert-2 explicitly says the project was not part of a larger transformation program — 'it wasn't part of some grand ERP-style transformation program' — cutting against the assumption that ITSM purchases ride on wider digital transformation budgets.
expert-2 has AIOps licensed-but-off and 'evaluating'; expert-1's small-company tool was chosen precisely for AI-first Teams integration. AI maturity is a live variable, not a settled feature.
expert-1 names an unprompted consequence of dropping the platform: 'we don’t really have asset management for all our IT assets, which is a big pain point for me right now.'
gaps: Only expert-1 and expert-2 discuss GxP-specific change workflow in depth; expert-3 (SOC 2 only) gives no comparable detail, so that finding rests on two accounts.
No interviewee gives ticket volume trend over time or per-agent staffing here, so 'not scaling' claims cannot be quantified against actual load.
expert-3 was not asked which modules were rejected or about hosting choice beyond 'fully cloud', limiting comparison of deployment models.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three evaluated ServiceNow and ranked criteria by size: the $40B enterprise put scalability and integration first and accepted a premium, while both mid-market buyers put total cost of ownership at number one and ruled ServiceNow out — one on cost alone, the other because it quoted nearly triple a comparable BMC bundle. Implementation speed and small-team administrability appear only in the smaller shops' lists.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow's capability is not in dispute; its price is. Both mid-market buyers acknowledge it as the strongest platform while rejecting it as disproportionate to their size.

positions.gist: Rated ServiceNow excellent but roughly triple the BMC quote for a comparable module set — indefensible internally.

citation.quote: Honestly, it came down to price relative to capability.

positions.gist: Eliminated ServiceNow early on cost, describing it as more platform than needed.

citation.quote: We ruled out ServiceNow pretty quickly on cost; it felt like way more platform than we needed at our size.

positions.gist: Agrees ServiceNow was priced above rivals but says integration, scalability and customization outweighed cost at enterprise scale.

citation.quote: They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.

agreements.statement: Jira Service Management was considered and dropped by both interviewees who looked at it, for the same reason: insufficient depth for CMDB, compliance and heavy ITSM workflows despite attractive pricing.

positions.gist: Jira lacked needed modules and was expected to hit performance limits at 1-2M tickets, despite being the cheapest option.

citation.quote: Jira is great for agile software project management, but we worried about handling infrastructure issues, major incident management, and change management.

positions.gist: Ruled Jira out early for lacking CMDB and compliance workflow depth.

citation.quote: We also briefly looked at Jira Service Management but ruled it out pretty early - it just didn't have the depth we needed for CMDB and compliance workflows.

agreements.statement: Integration with the existing HR/identity stack was a named top-five criterion for all three, though the specific systems differ (Workday/IAM, SAP plus Workday, Azure AD plus Intune).

positions.gist: Ranked integration capability first among the top five and demanded a POC proving Workday onboarding flow-through.

citation.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems.

positions.gist: Named integration with SAP and Workday as a core criterion, ranked fourth of five.

citation.quote: integration with our existing systems like SAP and Workday

positions.gist: Ranked Azure AD and Intune integration fifth of five.

citation.quote: Fifth, integration with Azure AD and Intune.

conflicts.statement: Where cost belongs in the ranking. expert-1 places TCO third behind integration and scalability; expert-2 and expert-3 both place it first and treat it as decisive.

positions.gist: Scalability was the single top criterion — 2M tickets a year would break the incumbent — with cost third.

citation.quote: So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.

positions.gist: TCO first, explicitly because of company size.

citation.quote: Cost was definitely near the top, just given our size - we're not a $40 billion company, we're a few hundred million in revenue.

positions.gist: Cost first without qualification.

citation.quote: Cost was number one, no question, given our size.

conflicts.explains_it: Company size and ticket volume: at 2M tickets across 2,000 sites, platform failure risk dominates price; at 18k-60k tickets, price dominates.

conflicts.statement: Ivanti's viability. expert-2 found Ivanti price-competitive with BMC and a genuine runner-up; expert-3, drawing on hands-on prior use, dismissed it as clunky and slow to configure.

positions.gist: Ivanti was close to BMC on price and general ITSM function, losing only on pre-built regulated-industry compliance content.

citation.quote: Ivanti was close in price to BMC, but their compliance and change-approval workflows needed more custom configuration to meet our GxP requirements.

positions.gist: Rejected Ivanti on the strength of a bad prior-employer experience with administration and configuration.

citation.quote: Ivanti I already knew from my last job, and honestly it wasn't a great memory - clunky admin, slow to configure.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2 judged Ivanti from a vendor evaluation and quote; expert-3 judged it from lived administrative experience at a prior job.

conflicts.statement: Freshservice's adequacy. expert-2 dropped it fast for a thin compliance workflow story despite the lowest price; expert-3 selected it as the sweet spot.

positions.gist: Cheapest quote but weak compliance workflow, so it fell down the list quickly.

citation.quote: Freshservice was cheapest but their compliance workflow story was thinner, so it dropped down our list fast.

positions.gist: Chose Freshservice for modern UI, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a workable price.

citation.quote: Freshservice hit the sweet spot: modern interface, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a price point that made sense for us.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2 needed GxP electronic-signature change control for a pharma auditor; expert-3's compliance bar was SOC 2 for financing partners.

outliers.gist: The only interviewee describing a formal proof-driven process — demo, then references, then a scoped POC in the vendor's environment — and mapping approval from director through VP to CIO.

citation.quote: In their environment, they’d run a small POC: here’s ServiceNow integrated with Workday—when a new employee is onboarded, it flows right into the ServiceNow process.

outliers.gist: Only one to describe a pricing-transparency tactic: demanding multi-year quotes from all four vendors to expose year-two and year-three escalation.

citation.quote: We asked all four vendors for detailed multi-year quotes, not just year-one pricing, because we'd heard stories about year-two and year-three increases.

notable: Two independent, roughly consistent price anchors: expert-1 indexes ServiceNow at ~$100/user/month against Zendesk at $50-55 and Jira at $20-21; expert-2 reports ServiceNow at 'almost triple our BMC quote' for a comparable module set.
expert-1 states the finance review was largely a formality: the case 'was presented to finance mainly to confirm budget alignment, but the real decision-makers were senior IT leadership.'
Administrability surfaces only below enterprise scale: expert-2 ranks 'ease of administration for a small team' fifth and cites a three-person platform team.

expert-1's own scorecard places ServiceNow below rivals on user experience (7 vs 8 for Jira, Zendesk and BMC) and lowest of four on TCO (6) — an unprompted concession from the platform's strongest advocate here.
Both mid-market buyers put implementation speed in their top three; the enterprise buyer never names it as a criterion at all.
gaps: Only expert-2 probed multi-year pricing escalation; expert-1 and expert-3 give no renewal-pricing view, so nothing can be said about how quotes held up over the term.
expert-3 gives no dollar or ratio pricing figures, only rankings, so the mid-market price gap rests on expert-2's single 'almost triple' comparison.
Neither expert-2 nor expert-3 describes a POC or reference-check step, so it is unclear whether they validated vendor claims before signing.
No interviewee discusses procurement, legal or security review as a gate, leaving the non-IT parts of the buying process unexamined.

columns_synthesis.headline: The two interviewees who scored vendors produce a consistent shape: ServiceNow tops integration (9 from both) and raw capability, and bottoms out on TCO (5 and 4) and administrability (6 from both); the incumbent each chose scores highest on ease of use and cost. The differentiator each names for their own pick is fit, not features — pharma-specific pre-built compliance content for BMC, cost plus ten-week time-to-value for Freshservice.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow is probably a 9 in raw capability, but you have to build a lot of it yourself.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow is strongest on integration breadth and raw capability but rates poorly on cost and on manageability for a small team — described by both scorers as powerful-but-complex and something you must build yourself.

positions.gist: Scores ServiceNow 9 integration / 5 TCO / 6 administrability, crediting a bigger connector ecosystem.

citation.quote: ServiceNow is powerful but complex, I'd put it at a 6 for a team our size.

positions.gist: Scores ServiceNow 9 on integration capability, 4 on TCO for their size, and 6 on ease of use.

citation.quote: ServiceNow I'd put at a 6 - powerful but a lot to configure.

positions.gist: Confirms the cost-versus-capability trade from the enterprise side and concedes heavier maintenance than competitors.

citation.quote: There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system.

agreements.statement: Zendesk is the simplicity leader and the asset-management laggard — strong user experience, but not built for internal IT asset tracking or ITIL process.

positions.gist: Credits Zendesk with deliberately simple UX and easy maintenance, but only 6 on customization.

citation.quote: And Zendesk is simple—they keep the user experience simple, which makes it easier for users and simpler to maintain with straightforward workflows. That's an advantage.

positions.gist: Names Zendesk the closest rival on ease of use (8) but scores its asset management a 3 and says it isn't built around ITIL.

citation.quote: Where Freshservice pulls ahead is asset management and the IT-specific workflows - ITIL processes that Zendesk just isn't built around.

agreements.statement: BMC is positioned as ServiceNow's nearest functional substitute, though for different reasons at different scales.

positions.gist: Names BMC the closest competitor to ServiceNow on customization, scalability and integration.

citation.quote: Probably BMC comes closest.

positions.gist: Scores BMC just below ServiceNow on integration (8 vs 9), above it on TCO and administrability, and ahead on compliance fit for their case.

citation.quote: BMC I'd rate an 8 for us specifically, because of the pharma-specific templates they had available.

agreements.statement: Each interviewee volunteers a real weakness in the platform they chose or advocate, rather than defending it outright.

positions.gist: Admits ServiceNow needed 3-5 staff at 30-40% time plus partners, and that this slightly affected ROI.

citation.quote: It was about 3-5 employees, each allocated around 30-40% of their time to maintain the system.

positions.gist: Concedes BMC's smaller partner pool delayed finding integrators with the right specific experience.

citation.quote: When we needed a specialized integration, our BMC partner pool was smaller, and it sometimes took longer to find someone who'd done exactly what we needed.

positions.gist: Concedes Freshservice's automation builder gets clunky with heavily chained conditional logic in complex approval chains.

citation.quote: It's not a hard wall, but you notice the automation builder gets clunky once you're chaining a lot of conditional logic.

conflicts.statement: Freshservice's fitness for depth work. expert-3 rates its asset capability a solid 7 with a good discovery agent; expert-2 rates Freshservice weakest of four at 4 in the equivalent area, calling it built for lighter-weight support.

positions.gist: Scores Freshservice 4 — weakest of four — for regulated workflow capability, built for lighter-weight IT support.

citation.quote: Freshservice is weaker here, maybe a 4; it's really built more for lighter-weight IT support use cases.

positions.gist: Scores Freshservice 7 with a solid discovery agent, explicitly good enough for their needs.

citation.quote: Freshservice I'd say a 7 - solid discovery agent, good enough for our needs.

conflicts.explains_it: Different dimensions and different bars: expert-2 scores GxP compliance depth for an audited pharma setting; expert-3 scores field-hardware tracking against 'good enough for our needs'.

conflicts.statement: Ivanti's competence. expert-2 scores Ivanti mid-pack and workable (7 integration, 6 compliance); expert-3, from direct prior use, scores it lowest of four on ease of use (5) and 6 on integration with lots of manual config.

positions.gist: Treats Ivanti as the genuine runner-up, close on cost and general ITSM function.

citation.quote: Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality.

positions.gist: Scores Ivanti bottom of the field on ease of use and criticises its integration for manual configuration.

citation.quote: Ivanti was a 6 in my experience, lots of manual config.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-3 scores from hands-on administration at a previous employer; expert-2 scores from an evaluation cycle. Same product, different depth of exposure.

outliers.gist: The only interviewee assessing vendors as a business rather than a product — CEO quality, market cap growth, the Moveworks acquisition, and a move toward CRM and Salesforce competition.

citation.quote: I admire that they're leaning headfirst into AI—now they have agents, and with the Moveworks acquisition as well.

notable: The two scorecards converge on ServiceNow integration at exactly 9/10 and administrability/ease of use at exactly 6/10 — independent agreement from a BMC buyer and a Freshservice buyer.
TCO scores for ServiceNow fall as the buyer shrinks (expert-2: 5; expert-3: 4; expert-1's own scorecard: 6), suggesting the perceived cost penalty grows with smaller size.
expert-3 supplies the clearest quantified trade-off: live in about ten weeks versus an estimated six-plus months and 'multiples' of the cost on ServiceNow.

expert-2's stated differentiator is not software but the vendor account team's domain fluency — 'They understood our GxP language without us having to explain it from scratch, which sped up implementation.'

expert-1 notes ServiceNow was not AI-forward at the time of his company's later switch to a custom tool, and that the chosen vendor was AI-first with lower licensing cost — an opening he says has since narrowed.
expert-1 flags Jira as newly competitive specifically because of AI, the only mention of AI shifting competitive ranking.
gaps: expert-1's numeric ratings sit largely in the vendor-selection column, so his scores are not directly parallel here; cross-reading requires care.
No two interviewees score the same vendor set: only ServiceNow and Ivanti are scored by both expert-2 and expert-3.
expert-3 offers no view on BMC and expert-2 none on Zendesk, so neither product is assessed by more than one person.
Only expert-1 quantifies ongoing administrative headcount (3-5 people at 30-40% time), so support cost per platform cannot be compared.

columns_synthesis.headline: Timelines span an order of magnitude — ten weeks, seven months, and 9-12 months against a 6-7 month expectation — and the platform itself was rarely the obstacle. HR/identity connectors went in natively in every case, while ERP or device-management data (SAP, legacy ERP via Databricks, Intune custom fields) all needed hand-built API or scripting work. The two smaller shops name end-user adoption as the hardest problem; the enterprise names scope definition and integrator estimation.

canonical_quote.quote: The biggest challenge honestly wasn't the platform - it was getting field staff to actually use tickets instead of texting or calling me directly.

agreements.statement: A hybrid integration reality: native or marketplace connectors handled identity and HR sync easily, but at least one core business system in every case needed custom API or scripting work the connectors could not cover.

positions.gist: Out-of-the-box APIs existed but legacy systems weren't reachable, so they built a middle layer and a custom API to join legacy ERP data in Databricks to service tickets.

citation.quote: They had some out-of-the-box APIs, but we had legacy systems and tools that those APIs wouldn’t connect to, so we built a middle layer to make them talk.

positions.gist: Workday went in on BMC's native connector; a customized SAP inventory instance required custom REST API work by an internal engineer.

citation.quote: For SAP it was custom REST API work built by our integration engineer, because our SAP instance is fairly customized on the inventory side.

positions.gist: Azure AD sync was native and took about a day; Intune needed native integration plus manual scripting to map custom fields.

citation.quote: we ended up using a combination of the native integration plus some manual scripting to get certain custom fields to map correctly

agreements.statement: Custom integration and scope work consumed time that had not been budgeted; both who quantified it describe a schedule overrun rather than a technical failure.

positions.gist: Expected 6-7 months, took 9-12 — roughly an extra quarter absorbed.

citation.quote: we expected a 6-7 month implementation, and it ended up taking 9-12 months—roughly another quarter we had to absorb

positions.gist: The SAP custom API added six or seven weeks that were never in the original budget.

citation.quote: That took an extra six or seven weeks we hadn't originally budgeted.

agreements.statement: End-user resistance to the new intake channel was a first-order implementation problem requiring a deliberate change-management campaign.

positions.gist: Site staff resisted the new portal; lunch-and-learns and walkthrough videos were needed, and volume through correct channels took two months to stabilize.

citation.quote: a lot of site-level staff had used the old portal for years and were resistant to a new interface

positions.gist: Field staff kept texting and calling instead of raising tickets, forcing an adoption push with incentives.

citation.quote: We had to do a real change management push, incentivize adoption, that kind of thing.

conflicts.statement: Whether the hardest part is people or scope. expert-2 and expert-3 identify data migration and user adoption as the top challenges; expert-1 identifies undefined scope, no definition of done, and integrator underestimation, and never mentions user resistance.

positions.gist: Points to fuzzy scope from heavy customization, an absent definition of done, and underestimated internal effort including unplanned user testing.

citation.quote: The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required.

positions.gist: Names data migration out of the legacy tool as the biggest challenge and end-user change management second.

citation.quote: The biggest challenge was data migration - pulling asset and ticket history out of the legacy ManageEngine tool.

positions.gist: Says the platform was not the problem; behaviour change in the field workforce was.

citation.quote: Like I said, about ten weeks from contract to go-live.

conflicts.explains_it: Scale and customization: a 2,000-site heavily customized enterprise build creates scope and integrator-management risk a ten-week out-of-the-box rollout for 450 employees never meets.

outliers.gist: The only interviewee attributing overrun to a structural gap between the vendor's playbook and its partner ecosystem's estimates, rather than to his own team or users.

citation.quote: I think there’s misalignment between ServiceNow and the partner ecosystem on how long things really take.

outliers.gist: Only one who used vendor marketplace apps as the default integration route, reserving custom scripting for a narrow gap.

citation.quote: Mostly the marketplace apps for the core stuff - Azure AD, Slack for notifications, a couple of monitoring tool integrations.

notable: expert-2 is the only interviewee whose implementation beat expectations — 'about seven months from kickoff to go-live, which was faster than I expected going in' — and the only one with a structured post-go-live adoption program and a measured two-month stabilization.
Legacy data export tooling is an underrated cost: expert-2 reports the ManageEngine export tools 'weren't great,' forcing manual cleanup and mapping before loading the new CMDB.
expert-1 notes prebuilt integration options simply did not exist then — 'at the time that wasn’t available, so it was mostly custom work using direct APIs' — which dates his experience.
Custom work clusters around ERP and device data, while HR and identity (Workday, Active Directory SSO, Azure AD) went in comparatively cleanly in all three accounts.
Only expert-1 mentions unplanned internal user-testing resource as a cost — resources 'who weren’t expecting it, and it was hard to secure their time.'
gaps: Neither expert-2 nor expert-3 discusses using an external systems integrator, so expert-1's central claim about vendor/partner estimation misalignment cannot be corroborated or challenged.
expert-1 and expert-3 say nothing about migrating historical ticket or asset data, leaving expert-2's data-migration pain point as a single account.
No interviewee gives implementation cost or professional-services spend, so timeline differences cannot be converted into a cost comparison.
Only expert-2 quantifies post-go-live adoption recovery, so the true cost of change management at enterprise scale is unmeasured here.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three overran budget, but by very different magnitudes — roughly 5% (Freshservice), ~15% (BMC Helix), and 'roughly double' competitors on implementation TCO (ServiceNow) — and all three were hit by a module they assumed was included but had to buy separately. The two who gave per-user pricing put ServiceNow at three to four times their own blended rate. Renewal uplifts cluster in the 4–8% range.

canonical_quote.quote: If I put BMC at roughly sixty dollars a user per month blended across our license tiers, ServiceNow's quote came in closer to one-sixty for a comparable module set, Ivanti was around seventy, and Freshservice was in the thirty to thirty-five dollar range, but again, with less compliance depth.

agreements.statement: Each was surprised by add-on SKUs they had assumed were part of the base package, discovered at or after purchase.

citation.quote: that was a separate SKU we had to add mid-implementation once we realized site staff needed mobile ticket submission

positions.gist: Only the Project module was an unbudgeted add-on, and he still rates the pricing as transparent overall.

agreements.statement: Annual renewal increases have run in the mid-single digits and both describe them as manageable.

positions.gist: Two renewals in at 4–6% per year, manageable.

citation.quote: increases have been in the four to six percent range each year, which has been manageable

positions.gist: Two renewals in at 6–8%, more than he'd like but still manageable.

citation.quote: increases have been around 6 to 8 percent each time, which is a bit more than I'd like, but manageable

agreements.statement: Both competitor price soundings place ServiceNow at roughly three to four times the incumbent's per-user rate for comparable scope.

positions.gist: BMC ~$60/user/month vs ServiceNow ~$160 for a comparable module set.

citation.quote: ServiceNow's quote came in closer to one-sixty for a comparable module set

positions.gist: Freshservice ~$40/agent/month vs a ServiceNow quote north of $150.

citation.quote: We're on a tier that comes out to roughly forty dollars per agent per month. ServiceNow's quote for a comparable scope was north of one-fifty.

conflicts.statement: Whether cost overruns are dominated by licensing or by uncosted internal labour. Expert-1 says the largest miss was soft cost — business-user testing and validation adding 20–30% — while expert-2 and expert-3 attribute their overruns almost entirely to purchased items (integration work, extra licenses, extra seats).

positions.gist: Internal level of effort for validation was the biggest miss, a 20–30% soft cost on top of a doubled TCO.

citation.quote: the biggest miss was the internal level of effort and commitment—pulling additional resources for testing and validation. I’d say that added another 20-30% in cost. It’s soft cost, but we had to pull those resources away from other tasks.

positions.gist: The ~15% overrun is traced to SAP integration work and unscoped Digital Workplace licenses, with no internal-effort miss mentioned.

citation.quote: We came in roughly 15% over our initial budget, mostly because of the SAP integration work I mentioned, plus some additional Digital Workplace licenses we ended up needing that we hadn't originally scoped

citation.quote: Pretty close to budget, honestly - maybe 5% over, mostly because we added a few more agent seats than planned once field supervisors wanted access.

outliers.gist: The only one who never gives a per-user price and the only one whose overrun is described as a multiple rather than a percentage — 'roughly double' competitors on implementation TCO.

citation.quote: ServiceNow’s implementation total cost of ownership was roughly double compared to its competitors.

notable: Expert-1 quotes annual uplift of only 3-5% — the lowest of the three — which sits oddly against the doubled implementation TCO and suggests the pain was front-loaded rather than recurring.
Expert-2's own reading of the cheapest option is not purely price-based: Freshservice at $30-35 comes 'with less compliance depth', which is precisely the trade-off expert-3 lives with.
Expert-1's cell contains several 'Can you repeat the question?' and bare 'Yes' responses, so parts of that account are thin and depend on the interviewer's unrecorded prompts.

Both expert-2 and expert-3 volunteered that the add-on they missed was one they only realised they needed after go-live decisions (mobile submission; Project module) — i.e. scope discovery, not vendor concealment, in their telling.
gaps: Only expert-2 and expert-3 gave per-user/per-agent pricing; expert-1 gave no unit price, so the three cannot be placed on a single cost scale.
Nobody was asked for implementation-services cost separately from licence cost, so 'total cost of ownership' means different components in each account.
Expert-1's role-separation and licensing-tier answers are fragmentary, and no equivalent question on role/tier licensing appears to have been put to expert-2 or expert-3.

columns_synthesis.headline: Satisfaction scores are tightly clustered (9, 8, 8) but recommendation scores diverge (9, 7, 9) and each caveat is platform-specific: ServiceNow is praised for power and faulted for cost and complexity, BMC for compliance depth but a thin partner ecosystem, Freshservice for ease and fit but weak reporting flex. Each named a concrete failure, and each traced it to their own platform's structural weakness rather than to bad luck.

canonical_quote.quote: I remember a manufacturing outage where people were trying to work through the major incident management process and didn’t know how to do it. They struggled with the ServiceNow flow, and it took 30-45 minutes just to create the ticket when it should be a 1-minute process.

agreements.statement: All three rate their platform highly overall (8–9) despite naming substantial, unresolved weaknesses — satisfaction is not contingent on the gaps being fixed.

positions.gist: 9/10 while listing cost, learning curve and implementation complexity as real problems.

citation.quote: I would say it's a 9 - 9 out of 10. Extremely likely.

positions.gist: 8/10 satisfaction but drops to 7 on recommendation because of the partner ecosystem.

citation.quote: Probably a 7. I'd recommend it with caveats about the partner ecosystem being smaller.

positions.gist: 8/10 satisfaction and 9 on recommendation, framed explicitly as fit-for-size.

citation.quote: A 9. For our size and use case, it's been a really good fit.

agreements.statement: Both attribute their worst incident partly to the vendor rather than wholly to their own environment — expert-2 to BMC not flagging integration risk in the sales process, expert-3 to Freshservice's reporting not flexing without a paid analytics tier.

positions.gist: 'A bit of both': unusual SAP config, but BMC should have surfaced the risk pre-sale.

citation.quote: I do think BMC could have flagged that risk earlier in the sales process instead of us discovering it mid-implementation

positions.gist: 'A bit of both': the custom compliance format exceeded what native reporting can do without the add-on.

citation.quote: for a very specific custom compliance format, it just doesn't flex enough without going into their analytics add-on, which we haven't purchased

conflicts.statement: Whether a smaller/cheaper platform is a legitimate choice or a false economy. Expert-1, prompted on why others pick cheaper tools, pushes back and reframes the decision around scalability, integration and regulatory compliance; expert-3 defends exactly that cheaper choice as the right fit and rates it 9 to recommend.

positions.gist: Would challenge a cost-led choice and weigh scalability, integration and regulatory compliance instead.

citation.quote: I would push back and question why that's the case. Cost might be one reason, but I would look at scalability, integration, and especially compliance from a regulatory perspective.

positions.gist: Rates the lower-cost platform highly precisely on ease, speed and value for its size.

citation.quote: Ease of use, fast implementation, solid asset management for the price, and genuinely good customer support when we've had issues.

conflicts.explains_it: Organisational scale and regulatory exposure: expert-1's frame comes from a 2,000-site, ~2M-ticket enterprise; expert-3 runs ~450 employees and ~18,000 tickets.

outliers.gist: The only one no longer on the platform he rates 9 — he removed ServiceNow and reports a resulting asset-management gap, an admission that sits against his own high score.

citation.quote: Yes. Yes, we're struggling now. We got rid of ServiceNow, and that left a gap in terms of asset management.

notable: Expert-2 is the only one whose recommendation score is lower than his satisfaction score, and the gap is entirely about the ecosystem around the product rather than the product itself.

The named failures escalate in business impact but not in satisfaction penalty: a 30-45 minute delay reporting a manufacturing outage, a two-month go-live slip with dual systems running, and a quarterly Excel rebuild for a SOC 2 report.

Expert-1's remedy for his failure is training and partner enablement, not product change — 'Better partner integration, partner training, and maybe more visual walkthroughs' — which points at the same ecosystem theme expert-2 raises about BMC.

Expert-1's cell includes an agreement with something the interviewer said ('Yeah, I agree. I think that's really well put'), so part of that view is an endorsement of a prompt rather than an independently volunteered position.
gaps: Expert-1 was asked about switching lock-in and about why peers choose cheaper platforms; those prompts do not appear for expert-2 or expert-3, so his comparative framing has no counterpart.
No one was asked to score the vendor's support or roadmap separately, so the single 8-9 scores bundle product, support and price into one number.
Expert-1 is evaluating a platform at a previous employer and after removal; expert-2 and expert-3 are current live users, so the scores are not measuring the same thing.

columns_synthesis.headline: Self-rated switching difficulty tracks customisation and scale almost linearly — 7-8 for the heavily customised ServiceNow enterprise, 6 for BMC with custom CMDB and compliance logic, 4 for the lightly customised Freshservice shop — and all three anchor against ERP as the 10. Notably, both non-ServiceNow users name ServiceNow as where they would go, for near-identical reasons.

canonical_quote.quote: Probably ServiceNow at this point, just because if we're going to absorb switching costs anyway, I'd want the platform with the broadest long-term ecosystem and AI roadmap, assuming budget allowed it.

agreements.statement: If they switched, they would move to ServiceNow, reasoning that if switching costs must be absorbed at all, the platform with the longest runway is worth it.

positions.gist: ServiceNow, for the broadest ecosystem and AI roadmap, budget permitting.

citation.quote: if we're going to absorb switching costs anyway, I'd want the platform with the broadest long-term ecosystem and AI roadmap

positions.gist: ServiceNow, for the most long-term headroom, once big enough to justify the cost.

citation.quote: Probably ServiceNow, just because if we're big enough to justify switching costs, I'd want the platform with the most long-term headroom.

agreements.statement: A large single-renewal price jump is a named switching trigger, and both quantify it in the 25-50% range.

positions.gist: A 30-50% increase, to the point of being unbearable, plus significant performance issues.

citation.quote: Also, a 30-50% cost increase—where it becomes unbearable—would be another reason to switch.

positions.gist: 25% or more in a single renewal, or a compliance failure the platform can't remedy.

citation.quote: say 25% or more in a single renewal, or a serious compliance failure, like an audit finding that the platform itself couldn't support a required control

agreements.statement: Lock-in is real but distinctly below ERP; the binding constraint named is custom data structure and workflow logic rather than the tool itself.

positions.gist: 7-8, explicitly benchmarked below ERP at 10, with ~$1M-$1.5M and a year of implementation.

citation.quote: it's not as difficult as an ERP system—I'd put ERP at 10, a multi-million-dollar project that takes 2-3 years to switch. This would be around 7-8.

positions.gist: 6, also benchmarked against ERP, with custom CMDB and compliance logic as the sticking point.

citation.quote: It's not as entrenched as something like an ERP, but we've built a fair amount of custom CMDB structure and compliance workflow logic that would need to be rebuilt or migrated.

positions.gist: 4, and explicitly because the data model and integrations are not customised.

citation.quote: We're not deeply entangled - the integrations are fairly standard, and our data model isn't overly customized. It'd be a project, but not a nightmare.

outliers.gist: The only one whose leading switching trigger is growth rather than price or failure — he would re-evaluate if the organisation tripled in size.

citation.quote: If we scaled significantly, say tripled in size, I'd want to re-evaluate whether Freshservice's automation and reporting could keep up

notable: Expert-1 is the only one to put a currency figure and duration on switching: $1M-$1.5M and at least a year of implementation.

Expert-1's answer on what would pull him away is effectively the mirror image of the others' answer — lower implementation cost, AI, and data portability out of ServiceNow — so ServiceNow is simultaneously the named destination for two interviewees and the named departure point for the third.
The stated switching triggers (25-50% jumps) sit far above the renewal increases actually experienced (4-8%), implying none of the three is currently near a switching decision on price.
gaps: Expert-1 was not asked, or did not name, an alternative destination platform in the same terms as the others, so his 'lower implementation cost and leaning into AI' criteria are unattached to a specific vendor.
Expert-3 gives no cost or duration estimate for switching, so his '4 out of 10' cannot be cross-checked against expert-1's dollar figure.
None was asked about contractual exit terms, data-export rights or migration tooling, which would materially change these difficulty ratings.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three run the same ITSM core — Incident, Problem, Change, Service Request, Knowledge/Asset — on three different platforms, but at wildly different scale: ~2M tickets across 2,000 sites, ~60,000 across a dozen sites, and ~18,000 across 450 employees. The differences are in what sits beyond the core: HR, GRC and a full CMDB at the top end, a Digital Workplace front-end in the middle, and a recently enabled Project module at the smallest.

canonical_quote.quote: It was a very large implementation—about a $40B company with roughly 2,000 sites. We handled around 2M tickets annually.

agreements.statement: The deployed footprint is the classic ITSM core in every case — Incident, Problem, Change and Service Request are common to all three.

positions.gist: Incident, Request, Problem, Change and Knowledge, plus CMDB, Asset and Major Incident Management.

citation.quote: The modules we used included Incident, Request, Problem, Change, and Knowledge.

citation.quote: we use Incident, Problem, Change, Service Request Management, Knowledge, and the CMDB

positions.gist: Same core plus Asset Management and a newly enabled Project module.

citation.quote: We use Incident, Service Request, Change, Problem, Asset Management, and we recently turned on the Project module for some larger infrastructure rollouts.

agreements.statement: Advanced/AI-adjacent capability is deferred rather than deployed at the two current implementations — AIOps is being evaluated but not on, and the most recent expansion was a Project module rather than analytics.

positions.gist: Full AIOps suite is not turned on, still under evaluation.

citation.quote: We don't have the full AIOps suite turned on yet - that's something we're evaluating.

citation.quote: we recently turned on the Project module for some larger infrastructure rollouts

citation.quote: We also used HR—many HR service requests ran through ServiceNow. And we started implementing GRC as another module.

notable: Ticket volume per employee differs sharply where it can be computed: ~27 tickets per employee per year at expert-2's org (60,000 / 2,200) versus ~40 at expert-3's (18,000 / 450), which matters when reading their later views on automation and reporting load.
Expert-1's account is retrospective — 'I used ServiceNow at my previous stop, Thermo Fisher' — so his module list describes an estate he no longer operates.
Expert-3 notes an unmanaged inbound channel: a rotating pool of field contractors submitting via email-to-ticket, the only mention of a non-portal intake path.
Both current users are cloud-hosted, and expert-3 notes his platform effectively forces it: 'Freshservice doesn't really do on-prem.'
gaps: No employee count is given for expert-1's ServiceNow estate (only revenue, sites and ticket volume), so his scale cannot be normalised against the other two.
None was asked how long each module has been live or which were deployed at go-live versus added later, so 'deployed' covers both mature and just-enabled modules.
Agent/licensed-user counts, as distinct from total employees, are not given for expert-1 or expert-2, limiting comparison with the per-agent pricing discussed elsewhere.

Asset/CMDB visibility is the one driver all three name.

canonical_quote.quote: Honestly, it was chaos. Nothing was tracked, nothing had an SLA, and when we started scaling up project development, leadership wanted actual metrics

citation.quote: We also needed centralized management of all IT assets.

agreements.statement: Measurable service performance - SLAs and resolution speed - was a stated goal for the replacement.

citation.quote: The key drivers were faster resolution of IT tickets and reducing MTTR.

positions.gist: No SLAs existed at all; leadership wanted resolution metrics.

citation.quote: Nothing was tracked, nothing had an SLA

agreements.statement: An external audit/compliance regime created a change-control gap the old tool could not close.

notable: Three different legacy starting points are named - Zendesk (expert-1), ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus (expert-2), and effectively nothing at all (expert-3) - yet the failure modes converge on speed, asset visibility and reporting/audit.

expert-2 and expert-3 both describe the compliance driver as arriving from outside IT (Quality/Regulatory; financing partners via SOC 2), not as an IT preference.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three say the effort began below the strategic level - as site-level pain or an IT refresh - and was elevated only once a compliance or governance argument attached to it. They differ on how far it travelled: expert-1 describes escalation into a global multi-module digital transformation, while expert-2 and expert-3 describe a bounded project that gained an executive sponsor but never became a transformation programme.

canonical_quote.quote: It started as an IT-driven project, honestly. I inherited the legacy tool and it was falling apart - outages, tickets getting lost. Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated, and our VP of IT and our Head of Quality co-sponsored it. So it became bigger than just an IT refresh, but it wasn't part of some grand ERP-style transformation program.

agreements.statement: The initiative was bottom-up or IT-originated and only became strategic once a compliance/risk case was made and leadership picked it up.

citation.quote: Once I built the business case around compliance risk, it got elevated

positions.gist: SOC 2 coming from finance, not IT, is what made it strategic.

columns_synthesis.headline: The two who answered describe near-identical mechanics: a GxP flag set at change creation that triggers routing through Quality for review/approval, plus a durable audit trail the old tool could not produce. expert-1 adds that the platform itself was validated; expert-2 adds electronic signature as a gate before implementation.

canonical_quote.quote: When someone opens a change, they tag whether it's GxP-impacting, and that routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation.

agreements.statement: A GxP checkbox/flag on the change record is the mechanism that triggers a distinct, Quality-routed approval workflow - and neither legacy tool could do it.

positions.gist: Ticking the GxP box triggers specific routing and change workflows Zendesk did not have.

citation.quote: when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have.

positions.gist: Tagging a change as GxP-impacting routes it to Quality before implementation.

citation.quote: The big one is the change approval workflow tied to GxP flags.

agreements.statement: Quality functions as a mandatory downstream reviewer/approver in the IT change path.

positions.gist: IT change goes to Quality, which opens its own change for approval, review and testing.

citation.quote: Typically, you have an IT change that then goes to Quality; Quality opens a change, it gets approved and reviewed, you might have to do testing, etc.

positions.gist: Quality review plus e-signature is a hard gate before implementation.

citation.quote: routes it through Quality for review and electronic signature before it can move to implementation

notable: expert-1 is the only one to raise validation of the system itself - a distinct regulatory requirement from workflow capability, and one expert-2 does not mention.
expert-2 grounds the audit trail in what auditors actually ask for, and concedes the prior state bluntly: changes were tracked in email half the time.
Both describe the value as blocking implementation until approval, not merely documenting changes after the fact.
gaps: expert-3 was not asked, which is a real loss: their compliance driver was SOC 2 rather than GxP, so the column cannot show whether the same flag-and-route pattern serves a non-GxP audit regime.
Neither respondent was asked about the friction or delay these gates introduce, so only the benefit side is on record.

The two smaller buyers also foregrounded implementation speed and the burden on a thin admin team.
