columns_synthesis.headline: Forced into strict ranking, the two mid-market buyers both put cost/TCO first and implementation speed third, while the large-enterprise buyer ranked integration first and pushed cost to third. Integration appears in all three top fives but at rank one, four and five respectively - the same criterion carrying very different weight by company scale.

canonical_quote.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership.

agreements.statement: Both mid-market buyers rank cost/total cost of ownership first and implementation speed third.

positions.gist: TCO first, implementation speed third.

citation.quote: First would be total cost of ownership.

positions.gist: Cost first, implementation speed third.

citation.quote: First, cost. Second, ease of use. Third, implementation speed.

agreements.statement: All three place integration somewhere in the top five, so it is material to each even where it is not decisive.

positions.gist: Integration capabilities ranked first.

citation.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities.

positions.gist: Integration capability ranked fourth.

citation.quote: Fourth, integration capability.

positions.gist: Integration with Azure AD and Intune ranked fifth.

citation.quote: Fifth, integration with Azure AD and Intune.

conflicts.statement: Rank of integration versus cost. Expert-1 makes integration the single decisive criterion and cost only third; expert-2 and expert-3 invert this, with cost first and integration fourth or fifth.

positions.gist: At enterprise scale, integration outranks cost outright.

citation.quote: At that scale, it has to work with your other systems.

positions.gist: TCO first; integration drops to fourth.

citation.quote: Fourth, integration capability.

positions.gist: Cost first; integration last of the five.

citation.quote: First, cost.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-1 attributes the ranking to operating scale; the other two attribute theirs to being small enough that budget is the binding constraint.

outliers.gist: Only ranker to include scalability and customization in a top five; neither mid-market buyer names either.

citation.quote: The second is scalability.

notable: Expert-2's ranked list elevates compliance: out-of-the-box compliance workflow support is ranked second, above implementation speed and integration.

Comparing with col-03-02: expert-1's unranked answer led with functionality and user experience, but under forced ranking functionality disappears entirely and UX falls to fourth - the ranking exercise changed the picture, not just tidied it.
Expert-3's fifth-place item is named as specific products (Azure AD, Intune) rather than a general capability, suggesting a narrower integration requirement than the other two.
gaps: None of the three was asked how far apart the ranks are - a first and a fifth may be nearly tied or decisive, and the lists cannot distinguish this.
No respondent was asked whether the ranking is retrospective rationalisation or the weighting actually used at the time; expert-2's 'Let me think' suggests it was constructed in the interview.

columns_synthesis.headline: Only two of three answered, and because their number one criteria differ, so does the evidence they demanded: expert-1 required vendors to prove integration by building it - demo, then a live POC in the vendor's environment - while expert-2, whose top criterion was cost, required detailed multi-year quotes rather than any technical demonstration. Both describe a step designed to test a vendor claim rather than accept it.

canonical_quote.quote: If they said yes in the demo, we’d say, show us.

agreements.statement: Neither took the vendor's assertion at face value; each insisted on documentary or hands-on proof beyond the sales conversation - a POC in one case, multi-year pricing detail in the other.

positions.gist: Demo first, then a short POC in the vendor's environment to prove the integration actually works.

citation.quote: Next, a short POC to prove it.

positions.gist: Demanded multi-year quotes rather than year-one pricing, because of known back-loaded increases.

citation.quote: We asked all four vendors for detailed multi-year quotes, not just year-one pricing, because we'd heard stories about year-two and year-three increases.

outliers.gist: Only respondent describing a staged technical validation sequence - demo, then optional customer references, then a scoped POC with a concrete test case.

citation.quote: here’s ServiceNow integrated with Workday—when a new employee is onboarded, it flows right into the ServiceNow process

notable: Expert-2's cost evidence produced immediate vendor differentiation: a three-year lock from Ivanti, a comparable multi-year commitment from BMC, and self-reported transparency about escalation from ServiceNow's rep.
Expert-2 shows the number one criterion is not applied in isolation - Freshservice won on price but was demoted for a thin compliance workflow story, so the second-ranked criterion acted as a gate.
Expert-1 treats customer references as a fallback rather than a primary proof point, which cuts against the assumption that reference calls anchor enterprise evaluation.
gaps: Expert-3 was not asked this question, so there is no account of what evidence a cost-first, field-workforce buyer demanded - and expert-3's ranking most closely matches expert-2's, making the missing comparison the most informative one.
Neither respondent was asked whether any vendor failed the evidence test outright, so the discriminating power of the POC and the multi-year quote is unmeasured.

columns_synthesis.headline: Each buyer chose a different vendor, and each says the deciding factor was their own top-ranked criterion: expert-1 paid a premium for ServiceNow's integration, scalability and customization; expert-2 rejected ServiceNow at roughly triple the BMC quote and bought compliance-readiness per dollar; expert-3 chose Freshservice for asset management and interface at a workable price. Both who assessed Zendesk read it the same way.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow was excellent but it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set, and for our size, that wasn't defensible internally.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow is treated as capable but expensive - the same fact leads one buyer to pay the premium and another to walk away.

positions.gist: Chose ServiceNow knowing it cost more, and scores its TCO worst of the four.

citation.quote: They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.

positions.gist: Rated ServiceNow excellent but priced out of reach at their size.

citation.quote: Honestly, it came down to price relative to capability.

agreements.statement: Zendesk is characterised by both buyers who assessed it as fitting customer service rather than internal IT needs.

positions.gist: Intuitive for customer service and small-to-mid market, but short on advanced workflow automation and customization.

citation.quote: Zendesk is very intuitive for customer service and fits small to mid-market needs, but it lacks advanced workflow automation and customization.

positions.gist: Built for customer support, with weak asset management for internal IT.

citation.quote: Zendesk felt built more for customer support than internal IT - the asset management piece was weak.

agreements.statement: Both regulated-industry buyers made compliance/GxP workflow support a decisive discriminator rather than a nice-to-have.

positions.gist: The incumbent's ticket management failing GMP/GxP requirements was part of the business case for replacement.

citation.quote: ticket management wasn’t meeting GMP/GxP requirements

positions.gist: BMC won partly because its GxP-relevant workflows were already baked in from other pharma and med device customers.

citation.quote: BMC had more of that baked in already from working with other pharma and med device customers.

conflicts.statement: How much more expensive ServiceNow is than the alternatives. Expert-1 puts ServiceNow at roughly double Zendesk per user and rates BMC as similarly expensive; expert-2 reports a ServiceNow quote almost triple BMC for a comparable module set.

positions.gist: ServiceNow ~$100/user/month vs Zendesk $50-55; rates BMC as also very expensive.

citation.quote: If we set ServiceNow at about $100 per user/month as a baseline, I’d put Zendesk at roughly $50-55.

positions.gist: ServiceNow quoted at almost triple BMC for comparable modules.

citation.quote: it was almost triple our BMC quote for a comparable module set

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-1 gives generic per-user rates at Fortune 500 volume; expert-2 reports actual quotes received by a much smaller buyer for a specific module set.

conflicts.statement: Whether Ivanti is a credible option. Expert-2 found Ivanti price-competitive with BMC and only lost on compliance configuration effort; expert-3 excluded it on the basis of prior hands-on experience of clunky, slow administration.

positions.gist: Ivanti was close to BMC on price; the gap was custom configuration needed for GxP workflows.

citation.quote: Ivanti was close in price to BMC, but their compliance and change-approval workflows needed more custom configuration to meet our GxP requirements.

positions.gist: Ruled Ivanti out on remembered administrative pain from a previous employer.

citation.quote: Ivanti I already knew from my last job, and honestly it wasn't a great memory - clunky admin, slow to configure.

conflicts.explains_it: Expert-3 judges from prior operational experience of the product, expert-2 from current quotes and workflow fit; they are assessing different things about the same vendor.

outliers.gist: The only respondent to describe the internal approval machinery and to quantify the driver - ~2M tickets/year, 2,000 sites, growth from ~$20B to ~$30B - and the only one for whom cost was not the constraint.

citation.quote: When we left it, we were at around 2M tickets per year, and trying to do that on the previous system would just break it.

outliers.gist: The only decision driven partly by a personal prior-employer memory of a vendor rather than by evaluation evidence.

citation.quote: Freshservice hit the sweet spot: modern interface, built-in asset management with a discovery agent, and a price point that made sense for us.

notable: Expert-1 states that finance was largely a budget-confirmation step and that real influence sat with directors, senior directors and VPs, with CIO sign-off only above certain spend - a claim no other respondent corroborates.

Expert-1's 1-10 scores are internally revealing: ServiceNow scores highest on integration (9) and customization (9) but lowest of the four on TCO (6) and mid on UX (7) - the chosen vendor lost on two of the buyer's own stated criteria.

Freshservice appears in two evaluations with opposite outcomes: cheapest but dropped fast by expert-2 for a thin compliance story, and selected by expert-3 where compliance was not a stated requirement.
Expert-1 notes Jira was rejected despite being cheapest (~$20-21) on capability grounds - the same shape of trade-off expert-2 made against Freshservice.
gaps: Expert-2 and expert-3 were not asked for the comparative vendor scores or per-user pricing that expert-1 gave, so the numeric comparison rests on a single account.
No respondent was asked, post-implementation, whether the deciding factor held up in practice, so all three accounts are justifications of the choice rather than evidence about it.
Only expert-1 describes the approval chain and business case; the decision-making structures at the two mid-market firms are unrecorded.

The one real divergence is Freshservice: a 6 from the expert with no hands-on Freshservice deployment versus an 8 from the expert who actually ran its Azure AD sync.

positions.gist: ServiceNow a 9 on raw capability.

columns_synthesis.headline: On cost the two raters are close to identical - Freshservice 9, ServiceNow lowest (5 and 4) because of what it costs at scale - and both frame ServiceNow's weakness as a fit-to-company-size problem rather than a capability problem. The thread also carries ease-of-use and depth scores, where the ordering inverts: ServiceNow scores 9 on capability from both while scoring worst on cost.

canonical_quote.quote: ServiceNow's probably the strongest on paper, I'd give it a 9, but it's overkill for us.

agreements.statement: Freshservice is the TCO leader at 9, and ServiceNow the most expensive, penalised specifically for cost at scale / at their company size.

citation.quote: Freshservice would be a 9, BMC an 8, Ivanti a 7, and ServiceNow a 5, just given how expensive it gets at scale.

citation.quote: Freshservice a 9, Zendesk an 8, Ivanti a 7, ServiceNow a 4 for a company our size.

positions.gist: Freshservice weak at 4, too lightweight for regulated-industry needs.

citation.quote: Freshservice is weaker here, maybe a 4; it's really built more for lighter-weight IT support use cases.

conflicts.explains_it: expert-2 judges against pharma/regulated-industry template requirements, where BMC's pre-built content sets the bar; expert-3 judges against a smaller organisation's ordinary asset-management needs.

citation.quote: BMC I'd rate an 8 for us specifically, because of the pharma-specific templates they had available.

notable: Both raters give ServiceNow its highest score (9) and its lowest score (5/4) in the same breath - the numbers describe a capability/affordability trade-off, not a disagreement about the product.
expert-3's Zendesk scores swing hardest across sub-questions: 8 on cost and 8 on ease/experience, but 3 on asset management - 'Zendesk is weak here, a 3.'
expert-2 rates ServiceNow only a 6 on ease of use 'for a team our size', tying the score explicitly to team size rather than to the product.
gaps: expert-1 has no content in this thread, so no cost or ease-of-use scores from the ServiceNow-side perspective - the vendor rated worst on TCO by both other experts gets no defence here.
The five questions in this thread are answered as one block by each expert without labels, so which score belongs to which sub-question (ease of use, depth, asset management) has to be inferred.
BMC is scored by expert-2 only and Zendesk by expert-3 only, so neither has a second reading.

columns_synthesis.headline: Each expert names the competitor closest to their own platform, and in every case the closest rival is close on breadth or usability while the incumbent's remaining edge is something specialised: compliance content, ITIL/asset depth, or customisation and scale. expert-1 gives only bare labels; the other two spell out the mechanism.

canonical_quote.quote: Where BMC pulled ahead was specifically in how much pre-built compliance content they had for regulated industries.

agreements.statement: The nearest competitor matches on general/mainstream capability, and the incumbent's surviving advantage is narrow and domain-specific rather than broad.

positions.gist: Ivanti is close on cost and general ITSM; BMC's edge is pre-built regulated-industry compliance content.

citation.quote: Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality.

positions.gist: Zendesk matches on ease of use and UX; Freshservice's edge is asset management and ITIL workflows.

citation.quote: Where Freshservice pulls ahead is asset management and the IT-specific workflows - ITIL processes that Zendesk just isn't built around.

agreements.statement: BMC is identified as the closest competitor to ServiceNow by the ServiceNow-side expert, and BMC is the platform expert-2 speaks for - the two accounts place the same pair of products adjacent to each other.

positions.gist: Names BMC as ServiceNow's closest competitor, with the gap narrowest on customisation, scalability and integration.

citation.quote: Probably BMC comes closest.

positions.gist: From the BMC side, the closest rival named is Ivanti, not ServiceNow - the adjacency is not reciprocated.

citation.quote: Probably Ivanti. They're close on cost and on general ITSM functionality.

outliers.gist: Answers with three unelaborated nouns - customization, scalability, integration - giving no mechanism or example, unlike the other two.

citation.quote: Customization, scalability, and integration.

notable: The adjacency is asymmetric: expert-1 sees BMC as ServiceNow's closest competitor, but expert-2, speaking from BMC, points to Ivanti instead - each looks at the tier below rather than above.

expert-1's named gap areas (customization, scalability, integration) are the very dimensions expert-2 and expert-3 both score ServiceNow highest on elsewhere, which sits oddly with calling them the *smallest* gap.
gaps: expert-1's answer is too thin to test against the others - no evidence, no example, and 'Yes, agreed' style brevity means we cannot tell whether the three named areas are close because BMC is strong or because ServiceNow is not differentiating there.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three confirm the vulnerability put to them - 'Yes, agreed', 'Yes, that's fair', 'Yeah, that's fair' - but each confirms a different weakness for a different platform: ServiceNow's maintenance burden and complexity, BMC's thin partner/integrator pool, and Freshservice's automation builder buckling under chained conditional logic. Notably the two who validated a weakness both downgraded it to a manageable friction rather than a blocker.

canonical_quote.quote: It's not a hard wall, but you notice the automation builder gets clunky once you're chaining a lot of conditional logic.

agreements.statement: Each expert accepts the vulnerability characterisation put to them rather than disputing it - none pushes back on the framing.

positions.gist: Flat confirmation, then pivots to ServiceNow's strengths and leadership.

citation.quote: Yes, agreed.

positions.gist: Confirms BMC's smaller partner pool with a concrete sourcing experience.

citation.quote: Yes, that's fair. When we needed a specialized integration, our BMC partner pool was smaller, and it sometimes took longer to find someone who'd done exactly what we needed.

positions.gist: Confirms Freshservice's automation limits, encountered as complexity grew.

citation.quote: Yeah, that's fair.

agreements.statement: ServiceNow's ecosystem scale is cited as a benchmark by both a ServiceNow user and a BMC user - the former through needing dedicated admins and partners, the latter through the contrast with BMC's shallower integrator bench.

positions.gist: ServiceNow requires dedicated admins plus partners for advanced configuration and integrations.

citation.quote: You need dedicated admins, and partners for more advanced configurations and integrations.

positions.gist: ServiceNow's larger community and integrator choice is exactly what BMC lacked.

citation.quote: With ServiceNow, there's just a much bigger community and more integrators to choose from.

outliers.gist: The only respondent to go well beyond the question - CEO praise, market cap growth, the Moveworks acquisition, AI agents and CRM ambitions - and the only one to volunteer a maintenance cost admission against their own platform.

citation.quote: There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system.

notable: expert-1's admission that ServiceNow needs 'more than other competitors' in maintenance corroborates, from the inside, the cost and complexity scores expert-2 and expert-3 gave ServiceNow elsewhere.
expert-1 concedes competitors' advantages unprompted - Zendesk's simplicity and Jira's AI push - while still rating ServiceNow's functionality and scalability as very strong.
Both expert-2 and expert-3 soften the confirmed weakness with a qualifier: 'sometimes took longer' and 'not a hard wall' - agreement in principle, limited pain in practice.
The three cells concern three different platforms, so the shared 'yes' is agreement about the interview method, not about any one product.
gaps: Only expert-1 answered the follow-up sub-questions on maintenance burden and competitive positioning; expert-2 and expert-3 have single-paragraph responses, so the thread's later questions have no cross-case comparison.
No expert was asked to react to the vulnerability attributed to a platform they do not use, so none of these confirmations is independent corroboration of another's account.
One passage in expert-1's answer is marked [AUDIO UNKNOWN], leaving the market cap claim unverifiable.

columns_synthesis.headline: All three name a different edge, and none of them is product capability in the abstract: expert-1 points to an AI-first posture (plus lower licensing), expert-2 to vertical-specific compliance templates and an account team that already spoke GxP, expert-3 to raw speed to value (ten weeks vs an assumed six-plus months on ServiceNow). Notably, two of the three still fold cost back in despite the question asking them to go beyond price.

canonical_quote.quote: Cost, hands down, and time to value. We were live in about ten weeks. I don't think we'd have been live on ServiceNow in under six months, and it would've cost multiples of what we paid.

agreements.statement: The differentiator is about getting to value faster than a ServiceNow implementation would allow - through vendor domain familiarity in one case and sheer elapsed time in the other.

positions.gist: Vendor's pharma/med-device fluency meant no explaining GxP from scratch, which accelerated implementation.

citation.quote: They understood our GxP language without us having to explain it from scratch, which sped up implementation.

positions.gist: Live in ten weeks, which he doubts ServiceNow could have matched inside six months.

citation.quote: Cost, hands down, and time to value. We were live in about ten weeks.

agreements.statement: Price remained part of the answer even when explicitly excluded by the question.

positions.gist: Names AI-first approach as the major difference but immediately adds lower licensing costs.

citation.quote: Cost was also a factor—we saw lower licensing costs.

positions.gist: Leads with cost outright before adding time to value.

citation.quote: Cost, hands down, and time to value.

outliers.gist: The only one to concede the edge has since eroded - ServiceNow has closed the AI gap - and the only one to quantify ongoing internal cost against it.

citation.quote: At the time, they weren’t leaning into it as heavily; the vendor we chose was taking an AI-first approach. That was the major difference. Since then, I think they’ve grown in their AI capabilities.

notable: expert-1 discloses a standing run cost that partly offsets the licensing saving: 3-5 employees at 30-40% of their time, plus partners for major upgrades and complex flows, with a self-assessed 'slight' ROI impact.
expert-2's edge is not a feature at all but the account team's domain vocabulary - a differentiator a competitor could in principle hire away.
expert-3's ServiceNow comparison is counterfactual, not experienced ('I don't think we'd have been live'), so the six-month figure is an estimate rather than an observation.
gaps: Only expert-1 was probed on the internal staffing cost of running the chosen platform, so the ROI offset he describes cannot be checked against the other two.
None of the three describes a head-to-head technical evaluation against ServiceNow, so claims of edge rest on impressions and counterfactuals.

columns_synthesis.headline: Elapsed time varies by roughly a factor of five - ten weeks, seven months, nine to twelve months - and the character of the pain tracks the length: the long, heavily customized programme suffered scope and internal-effort failures, while the two shorter ones hit data migration and, above all, user behaviour. Both shorter implementers named change management; the longest did not.

canonical_quote.quote: The biggest challenge honestly wasn't the platform - it was getting field staff to actually use tickets instead of texting or calling me directly.

agreements.statement: The hardest part of rollout was people, not technology - resistance to using the new channel or interface.

positions.gist: Site-level staff had used the old portal for years and resisted the new interface.

citation.quote: The second challenge was change management with end users - a lot of site-level staff had used the old portal for years and were resistant to a new interface.

positions.gist: Explicitly says the platform wasn't the problem; getting field staff off texting and calling was.

citation.quote: We had to do a real change management push, incentivize adoption, that kind of thing.

conflicts.statement: Whether the platform/implementation itself or end-user adoption is the binding constraint on rollout. expert-1's difficulties were internal to the project - fuzzy scope, unresourced testing - whereas expert-3 states outright that the platform was not the challenge.

positions.gist: Customization made 'done' undefinable and internal effort was underestimated; the project itself was the problem.

citation.quote: The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required.

positions.gist: The platform side was a non-issue; the whole difficulty was user behaviour.

citation.quote: The biggest challenge honestly wasn't the platform - it was getting field staff to actually use tickets instead of texting or calling me directly.

conflicts.explains_it: Degree of customization and scope: expert-1 ran a heavily customized 9-12 month programme; expert-3 ran a ten-week deployment where field staff were previously contacting him directly.

outliers.gist: The only one to report the timeline beating expectations, and the only one whose top challenge was legacy data extraction rather than scope or adoption.

citation.quote: It took about seven months from kickoff to go-live, which was faster than I expected going in. The biggest challenge was data migration - pulling asset and ticket history out of the legacy ManageEngine tool.

notable: expert-1 is the only one to describe a resourcing failure rather than a technical one: testers 'weren’t expecting it' and their time was hard to secure - a symptom of undefined scope rather than a separate problem.
expert-2 was pleasantly surprised at seven months while expert-1 absorbed an overrun; the contrast is in expectation-setting as much as in duration.
Only expert-2 had a legacy tool (ManageEngine) with asset and ticket history to migrate, which is why data migration appears nowhere else.
gaps: Nobody was asked to quantify rollout cost or internal headcount in this thread, so the very different durations cannot be converted into comparable effort.
expert-1 does not say whether end-user adoption was an issue at all, so it is unknown whether the 9-12 month programme avoided the resistance the other two describe or simply did not surface it.

columns_synthesis.headline: A consistent split runs through all three accounts: identity/HR integrations went in easily or natively, while the system holding operational or device data required custom work. Only the effort scale differs - a day of Azure AD configuration at one end, engineers and an IAM team in prolonged API back-and-forth at the other.

canonical_quote.quote: Workday integration was fairly smooth - BMC had a solid connector for HR data sync, onboarding and offboarding trigger workflows. SAP was harder.

agreements.statement: Integration was bifurcated: directory/HR connectors worked more or less as supplied, but getting asset, equipment or device data into the CMDB needed bespoke scripting or a custom API.

positions.gist: Workday connector smooth; SAP inventory/equipment data into the CMDB required a custom REST integration.

citation.quote: there wasn't an out-of-the-box connector that fit our SAP configuration, so our internal team built a custom API integration. That took an extra six or seven weeks we hadn't originally budgeted.

positions.gist: Azure AD native and configured in a day; Intune device data into the asset CMDB needed manual scripting for custom fields.

citation.quote: Azure AD sync for user provisioning was straightforward, native integration, took maybe a day to configure. Intune was a bit more work

agreements.statement: Vendor-supplied connectors did not remove the need for internal engineering effort.

positions.gist: Integration worked but was not plug-and-play; APIs, permissions and changes on both sides consumed engineer and IAM time.

citation.quote: It wasn’t plug-and-play; our engineers and identity access management team had to do quite a bit of work.

positions.gist: Needed an integration engineer to build custom REST work for SAP despite the vendor's connector library.

citation.quote: our internal team built a custom API integration

conflicts.statement: How much friction Workday integration entails. expert-1 describes it as part of a build that took time and considerable engineering; expert-2 calls the Workday piece fairly smooth on a solid native connector.

positions.gist: SSO with Active Directory and Workday integrated well but took time and a lot of API back-and-forth.

citation.quote: We set up single sign-on with Active Directory and integrated Workday. It wasn’t plug-and-play

positions.gist: Workday was the easy one, handled by the vendor's connector including onboarding/offboarding triggers.

citation.quote: Workday integration was fairly smooth - BMC had a solid connector for HR data sync

conflicts.explains_it: Different platforms and eras: expert-1 built at a time before hub tooling and against legacy systems, while expert-2 used a BMC-supplied Workday connector.

outliers.gist: Reports integration effort in days rather than weeks or months, and the only one whose hard case was resolved by scripting rather than a built integration.

citation.quote: we ended up using a combination of the native integration plus some manual scripting to get certain custom fields to map correctly

notable: expert-2 is the only one to put a schedule cost on the hard integration: an unbudgeted six or seven weeks for SAP.

In both expert-2's and expert-3's accounts, the obstacle was local configuration rather than an absent connector - a customized SAP instance, custom Intune fields - suggesting vendor connector coverage fails at the edges rather than at the core.
expert-1's difficulty involved 'changes on both sides' and permissions, i.e. the integration required altering the source systems too, not just the ITSM platform.

findings.statement: ServiceNow functions here as an unpriced reference standard rather than a contested product. Its capability is never disputed — 9s on integration and depth from both scorers, worst on TCO and administrability — and both mid-market buyers reject it on price at selection while naming it as where they would go if they ever paid switching costs. The corpus thus frames today's choice as an economising compromise and ServiceNow as the deferred destination, which sits awkwardly with the 8-9 satisfaction both report on their current tools.

findings.statement: The named differentiators, the implementation pain and the residual weaknesses all sit outside the product feature list. What decided each purchase was pre-built vertical content, a vendor team that already spoke GxP, or elapsed time to value; what hurt in delivery was scope definition, user behaviour and connector gaps to ERP or device data; what limits them now is a thin partner bench or an automation builder that buckles. Feature comparison explains almost none of the variance across these columns.
